title: Banjo versus guitar and tenor banjo tuning
summary: St. Cyr advises banjo for what the public wants but prefers guitar, which was New Orleans' foundation; costs and tenor and plectrum banjo tuning.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: I was going to ask, like today, supposedly some kid wants to take up the guitar or banjo and wonders which is which, or if you were going to tell some kids that were getting a band together, which to use, guitar or banjo, which would you advise and why?
Well, I'd advise banjo because it's what the public wants. The music-loving public in a dance orchestra, they like the banjo in preference of guitar. But for myself, I prefer the guitar.
I think the guitar works in a rhythm section better.

It belongs there. It's the first rhythm instrument used in the Dixieland band. Banjo became popular around 1917. That is, down in New Orleans. It had been popular out east. They'd use them quite a bit. But down in New Orleans, the guitar was always the rhythm foundation of the band.

I suppose my kid then is going to get a banjo, takes your advice, and says, well, the public wants that. Would you advise him to get a regular four-string tenor banjo, or would you advise him to get a guitar banjo?

Well, I'd advise to get a tenor because a tenor is easier to find. You can buy a tenor most of the time, but the guitar is kind of a scarce instrument. They're not stocking them anymore. And you'd either have to let Dr. Shushaw and pay about $220. The banjo alone would cost him $180 to have it made in the guitar. And I guess with the case, the case must run him around about $60. The outfit might run around about $225, $230. And you'd have to have it made, especially a lot, that they don't stock them. So I'd advise him to get a tenor banjo.
Oh, and what about the five-string? Is that what's called pector banjo?
No, it's four-string. It's tuned the same as the five-string. It's only, it doesn't have that fifth string.
What's that fifth-string tune for you?
A G.
Is that a higher G or a low G?
No, it's a high G.
Because it's a short string.
Yeah, it's a high G.
That's a string of C, G, D, A.
And G.
And what G is that? The way up higher?
Yeah, it's a...
It's a seven-high?
It's an octave higher than the regular G.
Yeah, octave higher than that G. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. What's the plectrum banjo tuning?
The same with the exception of that fifth string. It's played identically the same as the regulation.
